title: Balak: a hired curse (Numbers 22:2–6)
hook: the king of Moab pays the prophet Balaam to curse Israel

segments.voice: Yesterday, a copper serpent on a pole, and the Mishnah's teaching that it was the looking up that healed. Your line was look up and live.

A glowing review of a hotel, written by someone the hotel paid. A study about sugar, funded by a sugar company. Behind each one sits a plain question worth asking before believing anything: who's paying for this? The Torah has a story built around that question. A new portion begins today, and for once the Israelites barely appear in it. The whole story happens on the other side of the hill, where a frightened king is reaching for his wallet.
screen: `A PAID REVIEW, A FUNDED STUDY.` → `WHO'S PAYING FOR THIS?` → `A FRIGHTENED KING, ACROSS THE HILL.`

segments.voice: Balak, son of Zippor, is king of Moab. He has seen what Israel did to the Amorites, and Moab is terrified. In the text's vivid picture, paraphrased, this crowd will lick up everything around us the way an ox licks up the grass of the field. So Balak doesn't raise an army. He hires a curse. He sends messengers to a seer named Balaam, son of Beor, who lives far off by the River: come and curse this people for me. Then the flattery that sounds like a sales pitch, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "for I know that he whom thou blessest is blessed, and he whom thou cursest is cursed." The elders set out with the fees for divination in their hands. Payment up front. Two surprises. First, Balaam may not be only a character in a story. Archaeologists at a site called Deir Alla, in Jordan, found an ancient plaster inscription that speaks of Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods. A seer by that name was remembered outside the Bible too. Second, the rabbis read Balaam as someone whose gift was for sale. In Pirkei Avot, they contrast the students of Abraham, who have a generous eye, a humble spirit and a modest appetite, with the students of Balaam, who have a grudging eye, a proud spirit and a greedy appetite. And notice the portion's name, taken from its opening words. It isn't Balaam, after the prophet. It's Balak, the man with the money.
screen: `BALAK: A KING AFRAID.` · `HE WHOM THOU CURSEST IS CURSED.` · `DEIR ALLA: BALAAM IN PLASTER.` · `NAMED FOR THE MAN WITH THE MONEY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one opinion you picked up recently, about a product, a person, the news, maybe even yourself, and trace it back to where it came from. Did someone gain by your believing it? There's no need to be cynical, since many opinions are honest; just look for the hand on the wallet, if there is one, and then let the question go.
Balak. The king of Moab who tried to buy a curse, and the name of the portion that tells the story of the prophet he hired.
Your line: who's paying. It's worth asking before believing anything. That's day four hundred sixty-one.

chat.says: Why is the portion called Balak, when Balaam's the prophet in it?
options: It's named from its opening words, about Balak, the king with the money.
Balak and Balaam are two names for the very same seer in the story.
The rabbis renamed it so Balaam's name would never be read aloud.
chat.meaning: Portions take their names from their opening words, and this one opens with Balak, son of Zippor, the frightened king who hires the curse.

notes: Numbers 22:6 JPS 1917: 'for I know that he whom thou blessest is blessed, and he whom thou cursest is cursed.' Confirm.
Numbers 22:4 (ox licking up grass) and 22:7 (rewards of divination) paraphrased.
Deir Alla: discovered 1967 (by a Dutch team), plaster inscription naming Balaam son of Beor; dated roughly ninth to eighth century BCE. Confirm dating.
Avot 5:19 numbering varies by edition (5:22 in some); confirm the three traits as paraphrased.
